title: Complement counting and inclusion–exclusion
transcript: The complement of an event is everything outside it. When that opposite set is simpler, count it and subtract from the whole. When an item satisfies two rules, the two rule totals overlap. Correct those overlaps before subtracting the union.

AMC practice can ask for at least one or for none. Those conditions are opposites inside the same sample space. A Mawa style extension may combine several rules for the same number. Show how many times a number is counted when it obeys more than one rule.
Write a string of four letters. Each position can be H or T. How many strings have at least one T? Consider how many strings have no T anywhere.
Every position has two choices. There are sixteen possible strings before the condition. Only the all-H string has no T. Subtract it to leave fifteen strings with at least one T.
In a class, eleven students play tennis, nine swim and four do both. How many do at least one? Someone in both activities still counts as a single student.
Adding the two activity totals gives twenty. It includes each of the four shared students twice. Remove one copy of the overlap. There are sixteen students who do at least one of the activities.
Consider integers from one through eighty-four, inclusive. How many are divisible by none of two, three and five? Count the union of the three unwanted lists first.

Count each individual list by the multiples up to eighty-four minus the multiples below the start. The three counts are forty-two, twenty-eight and sixteen. A shared number is a multiple of the least common multiple for that pair. Subtract the pair counts fourteen, eight and five to correct double counting. A triple match has been added three times and removed three times. Add the two triple matches back so that they contribute once.

There are sixty-one excluded integers after the overlap corrections. The whole inclusive range contains eighty-four integers. Subtract the excluded count once from the whole range, leaving twenty-three integers.

The opposite of at least one is zero. Exactly one can leave out outcomes where two or more rules are true. Three-way overlap belongs to all three pair intersections. Add it back after subtracting those intersections.

Define the whole set using the bounds in the question. Write the exact complementary condition. If the excluded rules overlap, correct the union first. Then subtract it once and check that the result is between zero and the total.
